USDCAD bounces off the 100 hour MA. Buyers remain in control.
body: USDCAD is taking a breather after its steady climb from the early-November low at 1.3929. The pair has traded in a 44-pip range today, below the roughly 63-pip average over the past month. The narrower range suggests consolidation as traders weigh the next move.

The low today reached 1.4274, just above the rising 100 hour moving average (blue line on the chart above), currently at 1.4271. That area also corresponds with the highs from last Thursday and Friday and provided a base yesterday before buyers pushed higher (see red numbered circles). .

That makes it a key downside barometer and increases it's importance going forward. Stay above, and buyers retain control. Move below, and sellers would have an opening for a deeper correction. Over the next day, watch that level for your trading clues and short term bias.

Earlier today, buyers extended above the swing highs from the first half of October between 1.42918 and 1.42986. That is close restance that if broken would have traders thinking there is more room to roam to the upside. Today, the break took the price to 1.43154—the highest level since April 2025—but momentum stalled.
The immediate challenge for buyers is to reclaim and hold above 1.42918–1.42986. Doing so would put today’s high at 1.43154 back in play.
A break above that high would open the door for further upside, with the daily chart highlighting the March and April 2025 swing highs between 1.4397 and 1.4413 as a broader target.
For now, the rising 100 hour moving average defines support, while 1.42918–1.42986 is the hurdle buyers need to clear to get the upside moving again.

news.title: Fed's Williams: The economy is getting stronger, inflation not moving in the right direction
body: New York Fed President John Williams is out with some fresh commentary, and the message is a classic mix of acknowledging the inflation headache while trying to keep the market from pricing in anything too aggressive.

The big takeaway here for traders is that line about avoiding "dramatic policy action." Coming off the back of this week's hot October CPI print—and with the market increasingly jittery about the Fed having to ramp up its hiking cycle after restarting it in September—Williams is effectively pouring cold water on the idea of a 50 bps move.

Still, you can't ignore the hawkish undertones. Admitting that tariff and energy shocks are spilling over into the broader data is a notable shift. Back in October, Williams was singing a much more patient tune, arguing there was "no need for urgency" ahead of the late-October FOMC meeting and suggesting he saw no need for hikes in 2027. While he was open to one more quarter-point hike before year-end back then, the tone today is noticeably more concerned about the stickiness of prices—even if he isn't ready to panic.
For the December 9 decision, a 25 bps hike remains the clear base case and it's fully priced into markets with a dwindling chance of 50 bps.

news.title: Flight to safety concerns from continued cyber issues send stocks lower, yields lower, gold higher, JPY and CHF up
body: Reports that the National Security Agency’s internal communications network is down have added uncertainty to trading. Reuters, citing CNN, reports that the scope is being investigated, with no immediate evidence of a cyberattack. reuters.com

There are also reports circulating about possible Gmail and Microsoft Outlook disruptions, although a fresh widespread outage has not been confirmed. Google’s status dashboard currently lists no incidents. google.com
The market reaction has been a move toward safety. Stocks have moved lower, gold has pushed higher, Treasury yields have backed away from their highs, and buyers have moved into the CHF and JPY.
The NASDAQ composite has fallen below 24,206.50, the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the end-of-March low to the October high.

That gives sellers another technical break to build on. Staying below the midpoint keeps the sellers more in control. Moving back above would take some of the pressure off and raise the risk of a failed break.
For now, that level becomes a close barometer for buyers and sellers.
Gold extended to a session high of $3,891.07, but remains below its falling 100 hour moving average at $3,906.46.
The flight-to-safety buying has helped. However, if the price is going higher, buyers need to get and stay above that moving average.
Until that happens, sellers still have a level to lean against. A sustained break above would give buyers more control and strengthen the technical case for a further recovery.
The US 10 year yield moved from a high near 5.158% to a low of 5.093% as Treasury buying picked up.
However, the yield remains above its rising 100 hour moving average at 5.087%. That is the first downside hurdle. Below that, the swing area between 5.00% and 5.03% becomes the next key target.
Those levels need to be broken to take more of the upside pressure off yields. The retreat is a step lower, but the technical picture has more work to do.
Inflation concerns also remain part of the backdrop following the import and export price data released earlier today.
The CHF and JPY have attracted buying against the USD over the last hour of trading as traders move toward traditional safe-haven currencies.

news.title: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."

news.title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem says four more rate hikes may be needed in coming months
body: St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation.
During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity.
"The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said.

Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April.

Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028.
To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed.

"Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows.

However, he said the more likely scenario is that "persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures" combine to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target, thus requiring further increases in the fed funds rate from its current range of 3.75%-4%.

"It would be preferable for a higher real policy rate to happen in a balanced way, driven both by lower inflation and a higher nominal policy rate," he said. "However, the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work."

news.title: investingLive European news wrap: Risk sentiment remains tentative amid hawkish Fed and US-Iran stalemate
body: The main highlight in the session was the UK labour market report. The data was generally mixed, with the unemployment rate falling to 4.6% and employment rising by a stronger than expected 156K. However, the ONS expressed concerns about survey composition, while October payrolls showed a 34K decline and vacancies continued to fall. Wage growth also moderated, with regular earnings slowing to 3.5% y/y from 3.7%, although total pay growth including bonuses eased to 3.6%. Public sector pay remained significantly stronger than private sector pay, while real regular wage growth was modest at just 0.4%.

This data didn't change anything for the Bank of England's outlook, as the central bank will likely seek further evidence that wage inflation is easing sustainably before gaining confidence in the broader inflation outlook. Markets are still pricing in an 89% probability of a rate hike in December and a cumulative 95 bps of tightening by the end of 2027.

We also got the November German ZEW survey which showed a stronger than expected improvement in economic sentiment, with the Economic Sentiment Index rising to 35.6 from 28.1 and the Expectations Index climbing to 26.5 from 18.5, while current conditions improved slightly to -33.2 but remained firmly negative. The recovery is being supported by rising manufacturing orders and lower oil prices, although the outlook remains uneven across sectors.

Government spending remains a key driver of activity, but concerns are growing over the sustainability of rising public debt. Eurozone expectations also improved, rising 8 points to 26.5, while current conditions remained weak at -14.7. The survey points to improving confidence but doesn't change the ECB outlook, with a December rate hike fully priced in and markets expecting at least one further increase next year.Lasty, Fed's Musalem delivered his usual hawkish remarks, warning of a meaningful risk that inflation will remain elevated unless the Fed acts soon, saying that several rate hikes are likely needed before spring. He argued that moving early is the best way to bring price pressures under control without damaging jobs and economic growth, while stressing that the Fed's resolve is important to maintaining confidence, as doubts could push bond yields higher. Despite the inflation concerns, Musalem remains optimistic that above-trend GDP growth can continue, noting that monetary policy and financial conditions are still providing tailwinds.
